question: On 22 February 2024, after an in-depth investigation, Galician journalist David Reinero revealed on the praza.gal news website that the Partido Popular Government, led by former Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy, had tried to strong-arm the European Union into not revealing or at least minimising its criticism of Spain’s official inquiry into the Alvia train accident in Santiago de Compostela in July 2013.

That enquiry found that responsibility for the accident – which had killed 81 people – lay solely with the train driver. Praza.gal revealed on its website in 2022 that the Minister of Public Works in 2013, Ana Pastor, had sent a letter to former Transport Commissioner Violeta Bulc warning her of ‘political measures’ should a report criticising Spain be published.

The outlet now reveals that José Manuel García-Margallo, who was the Minister for Foreign Affairs at that time and is now an MEP, put pressure on the then President of the European Commission, Jean-Claude Juncker, in this regard. In any event, almost 11 years after the accident, Spain has yet to carry out the independent technical investigation required under EU law.
Is the Commission aware of this serious interference by the Spanish Government at that time, which sought to muzzle an investigation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.7.2024) It is Commission policy not to comment on articles appearing in the press. The Commission would like to recall that under the existing legislative framework and in accordance with Article 20 of Directive 2016/7981, the obligation to carry out an investigation after any serious accident on the Union rail system rests fully with the Member States.

The investigation after the tragic rail accident in Santiago de Compostela was conducted by Spain’s Railway Accident Investigation Committee (CIAF). In 2017, following the tragic rail accident, the Commission asked the European Agency for Railways (ERA) to draft a report on the state of implementation of EU legislation on rail safety and interoperability in Spain.

That report identified several deficiencies, including in relation to the national investigation body2 and decided to launch infringement proceedings3 in 2019. The Spanish authorities committed to implement an action plan to address the deficiencies identified by ERA’s report and have informed the Commission regularly in the course of its execution.

The Commission has since then been monitoring closely progress in the implementation of the corrective measures contained in the action plan. In 2023, the Agency confirmed that the rectification measures under the action plan are now fully implemented, and Spain had rectified the situation of the Spanish national investigation body and brought it in line with EU legislation instating its independence.
This situation led the Commission to decide to close the pending infringement proceedings in March 2024.
